title: Integrated photonic-electronic computing with broad system advantage

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a programmable computing system that combines integrated optical processing and communication with electronics to deliver a substantial advantage across a diverse set of useful workloads. Light would perform suitable operations or carry information, while electronic components provide functions such as control, memory access and programming. The objective is a sustained reduction in the energy or total cost of completed computations at useful accuracy, throughput and reliability.

The essential advance would be making these parts work together efficiently at system scale. A fast optical operation alone does not establish this capability: useful programs also require data preparation, movement, storage, conversion and control. The supplied processor study provides a specialized technical starting point, including reconfigurable optical signal processing, but does not demonstrate the broader computing system envisioned here.

significance.text: Conditional impact synthesis: a large, sustained reduction in the energy or total cost of useful computation would reduce the resources needed to run consequential workloads. If those savings survived manufacturing, deployment and operation, they could make more computation economically accessible and expand what users can afford to compute. These are possible consequences of the proposed system advantage, not demonstrated outcomes of the supplied research.

The importance of the system boundary is illustrated by the reported processor: optical processing depended on configured weights, thermal programming and supporting electronic computation, with adaptive electronic control discussed as future work. An optical-core advantage therefore cannot simply be treated as an advantage for the complete application. The study establishes relevant specialized processing, without establishing broad workload coverage or complete-system savings.

Impact limits synthesis: broad advantage need not mean that every operation benefits from photonics or that the system replaces all electronic computing. Savings may depend on workload structure, required precision, utilization and the amount of data exchanged with electronic memory. Greater access would also depend on purchase prices, software availability and deployment constraints; lower operating energy alone would not guarantee it.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is scalable integration that preserves useful precision and programmability while retaining a substantial advantage after all supporting functions are included. The supplied manuscript identifies concrete barriers: chip area, insertion loss in microring resonators, driver requirements and growing control complexity. Optical loss can reduce processing accuracy, while expanding the number of controlled elements makes configuration and operation harder.

Thermal tuning and weight precision are additional constraints. The authors describe milliwatt-scale thermal tuning power and qualify its possible efficiency relative to digital signal processing by system scale. Achieving the intended weights accurately, maintaining them during operation and controlling larger processors efficiently remain relevant engineering challenges. The manuscript does not provide a complete energy or cost comparison that resolves these tradeoffs for a programmable computing system.

System-level synthesis: the broader breakthrough also requires efficient coordination with optical sources, converters, memory, electronic control, data movement, packaging and cooling, together with a practical way to program substantial workloads. These are necessary accounting and integration considerations for this concept. Their combined burden could determine whether an optical-core benefit survives, but the supplied evidence does not quantify that burden or establish that it erases the benefit.

current_state.text: Khaled and colleagues’ 2025 accepted manuscript, identified in the supplied research as dated 18 December 2025, reports an integrated hybrid multimode-multiwavelength photonic processor. It describes two four-channel proof-of-concept configurations for specialized signal processing, including real-time optical signal unscrambling and radio-frequency signal unjamming. These are relevant demonstrations of integrated photonic processing with potential for further scaling.

The scope of real-time operation needs care. Optical unscrambling occurred after weight configuration; for RF unjamming, the weights were estimated offline using Python before optical processing. The manuscript discusses future integration of FPGA-based adaptive electronic control. Its integration claim concerns the photonic processor and does not establish that all estimation, control and supporting computation already operated within a fully integrated, adaptive computing system.

The reported devices do not demonstrate a general-purpose computing system or the proposed broad end-to-end energy or total-cost advantage. Their four-channel scope and documented scaling constraints delimit what was achieved. The broader capability remains unestablished by this evidence; that limitation does not show that it is infeasible or invalidate the specialized demonstrations.

Evidence coverage limitation: the supplied review examined the full main-article text of the accepted manuscript, but did not inspect supplementary material or figure images. Numerical performance should therefore be understood as author-reported rather than independently verified here. The supplied freshness record contains no later search evidence, so this record cannot establish the field-wide state as of 1 November 2026 or exclude subsequent advances.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently benchmark a programmable integrated photonic-electronic system on a declared, diverse set of substantial workloads against competitive electronic systems. Define the workload coverage and what counts as a large advantage before testing. Compare systems at matched application accuracy, throughput and reliability, and report both the workloads that benefit and those that do not. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent benchmarks show large advantage across diverse workloads under matched conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accounting boundary: demonstrate the advantage in end-to-end energy or total cost, including optical sources, conversion, electronic control, memory, data movement, packaging and cooling. Include workload preparation, weight estimation, configuration and calibration whenever the application requires them. State measurement boundaries and cost assumptions explicitly so that excluded supporting work cannot be mistaken for a system saving.
completion_criteria.label: End-to-end energy or total cost advantage includes supporting work

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: provide enough hardware, software, workload and measurement detail for independent teams to reproduce the comparison. Demonstrate sustained operation and characterize how performance changes with precision, processor scale, workload changes and recalibration requirements. A convincing result would establish an advantage across the tested operating range; finite benchmarks would demonstrate breadth within that range, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible comparisons demonstrate sustained advantage across the tested operating range

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ELE-04, Practical, energy-recovering reversible computing, shares the goal of reducing the resource cost of useful computation. Its central mechanism is energy recovery and reversible computation; ELE-11 centers on integrated photonic-electronic architecture. Either could be pursued without the other. Combining them would require separate evidence that their mechanisms and supporting circuitry work together beneficially.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-08, Manufacturable ultra-low-voltage switching for general-purpose electronics, could address the energy of electronic components used alongside photonics. Its defining advance concerns electronic switching and manufacturing, whereas ELE-11 concerns the performance of an integrated computing system. Better switching could help the electronic portion without resolving optical loss, photonic precision or system integration.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-02, Fault-tolerant quantum computer with useful, scalable logical computation, and ELE-03, A long-distance quantum repeater network, concern quantum computation and quantum networking respectively. The optical signal-processing evidence supplied for ELE-11 does not establish either capability. Using photons in a computing architecture does not by itself imply quantum computation or quantum communication.

unresolved_issues: No supplied evidence establishes whether a programmable photonic-electronic system can deliver the proposed broad end-to-end advantage.
The combined energy and cost of optical sources, conversion, memory, control, data movement, packaging and cooling remain unquantified for the envisioned system.
The workload set, practical operating range and numerical threshold for a large advantage remain to be defined.
Scaling beyond the reported four-channel configurations while preserving precision and efficient control remains unresolved in this record.
Supplementary material and figure images were not inspected in the supplied review; reported numerical performance was not independently verified here.
The supplied research identifies 18 December 2025 as the manuscript date, but the supplied review does not separately establish the exact publication chronology.
The empty freshness record leaves later developments and field-wide status as of 1 November 2026 unresolved.

brief.title: Computers that save energy by using light
possible: People could run a wide range of useful programs with substantially less energy or lower total cost. A programmable computer would combine light, used for suitable calculations and communication, with electronics for memory and control.
why: Lower computing costs could let more people and organisations afford demanding workloads. Sustained savings would reduce the resources needed to run them and expand what users can afford to compute.

sources.showed: They built a chip that uses light to separate mixed signals and remove radio interference. Some supporting calculations happened separately, before optical processing.
sources.quote: Here, we present a scalable, monolithically integrated hybrid photonic processor
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates specialised signal processing using integrated optical components.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a programmable computer with broad savings after all supporting work is included.

sources.showed: They built a rack-mounted light-based processor that runs trained neural networks, models that learn patterns from data. It classified images through an electronic interface.
sources.quote: Packaged as a rack-mounted system with electronic I/O, calibration procedures, and PyTorch integration, the PTP executes pretrained networks on photonic hardware without chip-specific retraining.
sources.cited_for: The work connects optical calculations to practical software and demonstrates image classification.
sources.not_established: Image classification does not establish broad workload coverage or complete-system energy or cost savings.

sources.who: Shiyue Hua and colleagues at Lightelligence and Stanford University
sources.showed: They combined an optical computing chip with electronics for memory and control. The system contained more than 16,000 optical components and demonstrated fast searches for solutions to difficult optimisation problems.
sources.quote:
Logic, memory and control functions that support
photonic matrix MAC operations were designed into a cointegrated electronics chip.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates larger-scale integration and measures energy efficiency with laser power included.
sources.not_established: Results on selected optimisation problems do not establish sustained savings across diverse workloads.

sources.who: Zhizhen Zhong and colleagues at Massachusetts Institute of Technology
sources.showed: Their Lightning prototype combined optical computing with electronic control and served image-classification requests faster than comparison processors. Larger energy savings came from simulations.
sources.quote:
This coupling of the control
and data planes creates significant overhead in the datapath and
hurts end-to-end latency.
sources.cited_for: The work shows why moving data and coordinating calculations matter to complete-system performance.
sources.not_established: Simulated energy savings do not establish measured savings across diverse workloads at matched accuracy.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated specialised systems that combine light-based calculations with electronics. Hua and colleagues built a large integrated accelerator, while Meyer and colleagues connected a reprogrammable processor to software for running trained neural networks.

Zhong and colleagues demonstrated faster image-classification service with Lightning. These results show working pieces of the proposed capability; broad, sustained energy or total-cost savings remain unestablished.
missing: A programmable system still needs to demonstrate substantial savings across diverse useful workloads at matched accuracy, speed and reliability.
Complete measurements must include light sources, signal conversion, memory, control, data movement, preparation, packaging and cooling.
Larger processors must preserve calculation accuracy while keeping configuration, calibration and control efficient.
Independent teams must reproduce sustained savings across the tested operating range.

milestones.label: Independent tests show broad gains under matched conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent tests would have to show a predefined large advantage across diverse substantial workloads at matched accuracy, speed and reliability. This would establish breadth beyond specialised demonstrations.

milestones.label: Savings survive all supporting work
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to show lower energy use or total cost including all supporting equipment, preparation and operation. This would establish that savings survive beyond the optical calculations.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce sustained gains across tested conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce sustained gains as accuracy requirements, processor size, workloads and recalibration needs vary. This would establish the operating range in which the advantage holds.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether supporting equipment and electronic work will leave enough savings for a broad system advantage.
The workload set, operating range and threshold for a large advantage remain to be defined.
How far processors can grow while preserving accuracy and efficient control remains unresolved.

page.title: Integrated photonic-electronic computing with energy advantage
page.definition: A programmable computer combines integrated optical arithmetic with electronic memory and control, and uses less operating energy per completed task than electronic comparison systems across inference, signal processing and optimisation. Optical arithmetic performs calculations through the propagation and detection of light.

goal.need: Data centres consumed an estimated 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, about 1.5% of global electricity consumption. Photonic acceleration therefore targets an energy expenditure already measurable at electricity-system scale. Its accounting boundary matters: PACE reports different arithmetic efficiencies depending on whether laser power is included. Neither arithmetic efficiency alone establishes energy savings for completed applications.

figures.caption: PACE's reported arithmetic efficiency depends on the power boundary.
figures.note: TOPS/W means trillion operations per second per watt. These are accelerator arithmetic measurements, not energy measurements for complete applications.

statements.body: European Commission Horizon Europe programme: NEUROPULS
statements.quote: Three relevant use-cases will be considered for benchmarking to demonstrate 2 orders of magnitude energy efficiency improvement.
statements.context: The grant was signed on 24 November 2022. Its objective concerns programmable photonic neuromorphic accelerators for edge computing.

statements.quote: will deliver multiply-accumulate (MAC) performance at 3.2 PetaMAC/s at an energy cost of 50 FemtoJoule/MAC.
statements.context: The grant was signed on 1 December 2020. A multiply-accumulate operation multiplies two numbers and adds their product to an accumulated sum.

completion.title: Independent replication confirms energy savings across three computation classes on one photonic system.
completion.criterion: One programmable integrated photonic-electronic system uses less operating energy per completed task than the lowest-energy publicly measured electronic baselines identified when the test is registered. A preregistered suite spans neural-network inference, signal processing and optimisation. Each workload meets identical quality, throughput and error requirements. Every energy ratio is <1 after measurement uncertainty. Meter all required equipment and preparation, including lasers, conversion, memory, control, cooling, calibration and weight loading. An independent team reproduces the comparison. The suite and pass condition are Atlas choices.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside completion test covering this cross-domain capability was located.
completion.basis: Searches of Army STTR accelerator targets, Horizon NEUROPULS and PHOENICS objectives, and MLCommons benchmark and power rules found accelerator-specific targets and inference measurement protocols, but no replicated, cross-domain energy-advantage criterion. The fallback requires a strict energy reduction across the three demonstrated application classes without assigning an unsupported minimum advantage factor.

milestones.title: A photonic prototype delivers ≥2 TOPS at ≤0.5 W with matrix loading above 100 MHz.
milestones.criterion: An experimental photonic accelerator reaches ≥2 TOPS (10^12 operations/s), matrix loading >100 MHz and electrical power ≤0.5 W. Related laboratory evidence: Khaled and colleagues, published on 18 December 2025, demonstrated two four-channel configurations for signal processing, including optical signal unscrambling at 5 Gb/s with 30 ps optical processing latency. Those results do not establish the three accelerator requirements together.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Army, STTR 20.B topic A20B-T004, Phase I; written for neural-network accelerators.

milestones.title: An integrated photonic accelerator delivers ≥100 TOPS at ≤10 W with matrix loading above 500 MHz.
milestones.criterion: Fabricated integrated photonic hardware reaches ≥100 TOPS, matrix loading >500 MHz and electrical power ≤10 W. Related integration evidence: PACE, published on 9 April 2025, combines a 64 × 64 photonic matrix processor with electronic memory and control and reports approximately 8.19 TOPS. Its reported throughput is below this programme target.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Army, STTR 20.B topic A20B-T004, Phase II; written for neural-network accelerators.

milestones.title: One photonic-electronic system saves energy across inference, signal processing and optimisation.
milestones.criterion: The original team demonstrates the completion energy comparison across all three computation classes; independent replication remains outstanding. Related evidence: Lightning reports a 6.6-fold inference serve-time gain over an A100 for LeNet; its accuracy test gives 96.2% on 1,000 requests versus 97.45% on a GPU. Its 352-fold A100 energy saving comes from simulation. Meyer's rack system, published on 9 April 2026, reports 72% CIFAR-10 accuracy on 400 images. Neither paper establishes this cross-domain energy result.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: the searched programme targets and MLCommons rules provide no intermediate cross-domain system-energy test.

not_found: NEUROPULS's public objective does not specify the electronic baseline, accuracy requirements or complete energy boundary for its 100-fold target.
No measured, independently reproduced energy comparison spanning all three computation classes on one programmable photonic-electronic system was located.

results.finding: The photonic processor unscrambled two optical signal channels at 5 Gb/s.
results.detail: The experiment does not establish ≥2 TOPS, matrix loading above 100 MHz, and electrical power ≤0.5 W together. The signal data rate is not a matrix-loading rate.
results.quote:
Two emulated scrambled
signals are encoded on two mode channels (TE 0 and TE 1) and sent to the photonic processor at an
operating speed of 5 Gb/s.

results.finding: One photonic tensor processor reprogrammed its full weight array in 62 ms.
results.detail: The full-array update is far slower than the required matrix-loading rate. The paper projects 27 GMAC/s and 2.5 W for the 9 × 3 configuration, rather than demonstrating all three targets together.
results.quote: Reprogramming the full weight array takes 62 ms, whereas streaming inputs and digitizing outputs operate continuously at the RF-DAC/RF-ADC sample rates.

results.finding: One integrated photonic tensor processor reprogrammed its full weight array in 62 ms.
results.detail: The update is far slower than the required matrix-loading rate. The paper projects 27 GMAC/s for its 9 × 3 configuration; it does not demonstrate 100 TOPS.
results.quote: Reprogramming the full weight array takes 62 ms, whereas streaming inputs and digitizing outputs operate continuously at the RF-DAC/RF-ADC sample rates.

results.finding: Photonic inference achieved 72% accuracy on 400 CIFAR-10 images.
results.detail: The system demonstrates inference, but the paper does not establish an energy-per-task saving across inference, signal processing and optimisation.
results.quote: Photonic inference on a subset of 400 images reaches an accuracy of 72%.

results.finding: One PACE photonic accelerator achieved approximately 8.19 TOPS.
results.detail: Its weight modulators were designed for 10 MHz, below the matrix-loading requirement. The reported throughput and laser-inclusive efficiency imply approximately 3.44 W, above the power limit.
results.quote:
In the operation, the system can achieve a throughput 
of approximately 8.19 TOPS.

results.finding: One integrated PACE photonic accelerator achieved approximately 8.19 TOPS.
results.detail: Throughput is below 100 TOPS, and the weight modulators were designed for 10 MHz, below the matrix-loading requirement. Reported throughput and laser-inclusive efficiency imply approximately 3.44 W.
results.quote:
In the operation, the system can achieve a throughput 
of approximately 8.19 TOPS.

results.finding: Lightning simulations across seven DNN models report 352× less inference energy than an A100 GPU.
results.detail: The energy comparison is simulated and covers inference only; the team does not demonstrate energy savings across inference, signal processing and optimisation.
results.quote:
Our simula-
tions with large DNN models show that compared to Nvidia A100
GPU, A100X DPU, and Brainwave smartNIC, Lightning acceler-
ates the average inference serve time by 337×, 329×, and 42×, while
consuming 352×, 419×, and 54× less energy, respectively.

results.finding: One 16-channel photonic accelerator achieved a peak computational capacity of 1.92 TOPS.
results.detail: The reported peak falls below 2 TOPS. The paper reports 60 GBaud weight loading, but does not establish total electrical power of 0.5 W or less; near-zero static power is not total operating power.
results.quote: The chip achieves a computing speed of 120 GOPS with a peak computational capacity of 1.92 TOPS (derived from 60×2×4×4 operations).

results.finding: A 256 × 98 portion of a fabricated photonic chip reportedly achieved 1,000 TOPS.
results.detail: The reported result uses off-chip modulators at 20 GS/s; the text does not establish a matrix-loading rate above 500 MHz. The 8 W system power is an estimate for a 256 × 256 configuration, not a measurement of the demonstrated setup.
results.quote:
Homodyne signals were obtained 
up to column 98 (Fig. 3i-l), confirming the operability of at least 256 × 98 matrix operation and 1000 
TOPS at a clock rate of 20 GS/s.

results.finding: For image compression and reconstruction, the photonic-electronic processor used 3 orders of magnitude less energy than GPU comparisons; benchmark sample size not stated.
results.detail: This reports an estimated energy comparison for image processing, but does not demonstrate energy savings across inference, signal processing and optimisation on the same system. The compared reconstruction models differ.
